notes: Unadjusted, a doubling of supermarkets per resident goes with 0.895 (0.822 to 0.974) times the diabetes admission ratio, close to the graph's cross-sectional findings. Adjusted for residential density, poverty, income and median age the ratio is 0.995 (0.946 to 1.046). Secondary models: adding percent Black and percent Hispanic 0.993 (0.943 to 1.046); adding households without a car 0.987 (0.931 to 1.047); stores of 10,000 sq ft or more 0.978 (0.940 to 1.017); all retail food stores 0.994 (0.923 to 1.070). Chicken-and-egg check: supermarkets per km2 alone give 0.951 (0.905 to 0.999); adding log residential density gives 0.895 (0.822 to 0.975), which is algebraically the per-resident unadjusted estimate, so density explains the per-area pattern and per-resident supply then carries the crude association; that association disappears when poverty and income are added. In the primary model a 10-point rise in poverty goes with 1.22 (1.09 to 1.35) times the admission ratio; R2 0.67. Deviation from the committed script, before any outcome was read: the Census API now requires a key, so the same ACS 2019-2023 variables were read from the Census table-based summary files; the county filter for the store list was corrected to upper case after the first query returned no rows. Stores are counted by their address ZIP from the current list (October 2026), so openings and closings after 2023 add noise; two ZCTAs have no supermarket. Admissions measure access to primary care as well as disease. The cross-section cannot show what a new store would do; it shows that in New York the places with fewer supermarkets per resident do not have more diabetes admissions than their income and density predict.
notes_referee: Referee reproduced 0.995 (0.946 to 1.046); clustered and spatial-error models still meet support_if; Moran's I 0.35; lower bound 0.88 unweighted or with 2.5 km supply. Outcome tracks poverty and access to care: pneumonia and UTI admissions show the same crude gradient (0.885).
